Need for Reduction of GST on Kendu leaves for the State of Odisha 
SHRI SUBHASH CHANDRA  SINGH (Odisha):  "Sir, out of the 4.5 crore population 
of Odisha, 10 lakh people are engaged in Kendu leaf sector. A large section of people 
engaged in this sector are poor, Adivasis and Harijans. Most of them belong to the 
Western part of Odisha, and 80 per cent of them are women. Their financial condition 
is very weak. Sir, 18 per cent GST is levied on Kendu leaf.  In Odisha, prior to the

brought down to its earlier level , these poor Adivasi women and poor men who are 
engaged in this sector between the months of March to June and draw their livelihood 
and sustenance from the Kendu leaf, such women folk could be largely benefitted. 
Our hon. Chief Minister of Odisha Sh. Naveen Patnaik has already written twice to the 
Finance Minist ry and to the Chairman, GST. Some direction should come from the 
hon. Chairman in this matter. These 10 lakh people are engaged in this sector. Out of 
this 80 per cent are w omen. They will get benefitted by their earning with the increase 
in the bonus amou nt and further they would also get the benefit of security. I urge 
upon the hon. Chairman to direct the Central Government to take a decision to sort 
out the major problem o f the Kendu leaf workers,  and, accordingly, reduce the GST 
on Kendu leaf from 18 per cent to its earlier level of 5 per cent. Namaskar."

Statement 
(a) to (e) Considering the import ance of the clean air, Government has launched Air 
Quality Index (AQI) in the year 2015. 
Air Quality Index (AQI) provides air pollution status of an area or city but not that 
of any State. AQI of a city depends on multiple factors, which include meteorolo gy, 
geography, local sources such as vehicles, industries, etc. and contribution from 
other regional sources. 
Delhi with higher population, number of vehicles, emission from various other 
local sources as well as contribution of regional sources such as st ubble burning 
(during October, November), dust in summer has higher air pollution levels compared 
to many of the adjoining cities including cities of Punjab.  
With low winds, low temperatures and limited mixing area available for dilution, 
the pollution l evels in Delhi are higher during winter. In October and November, wind 
blows from Punjab towards Delhi. This brings pollution due to stubble burning towards 
Delhi and adds to Delhi’s pollution.  
It is observed that meteorology plays very important role in  air pollution. Other 
metropolitan cities like Chennai, Bengaluru and Mumbai have similar or more pollution 
sources as Delhi. But, air quality in these cities is far better than Delhi due to high 
winds and mixing zone and other meteorological factors.  
With ma ny actions taken by the Government such as introduction of BS -VI, 
expansion of Metro, operationalization of Eastern and Western peripheral 
expressways, shifting of industries to PNG, waste processing plants, online round the 
clock monitoring of red ca tegory industries, etc. Air quality has improved significantly 
in Delhi.  Details are given in the annexure.

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND CLIMATE CHANGE (SHRI PRAKASH 
JAVADEKAR): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) As a result of concerted efforts made for protection and conservation 
of wildlife, the population of several wildlife species like Tigers, Elephants, Asiatic 
Lion, Rhino etc. in the country has increased. There are reports of wild animals 
moving out of the forests leading to human wildlife conflict situations. 
The management of wildlife is primarily the responsibility of the concerned 
States/Union Territories.  
The important steps taken by Government of India to manage and mitigate human -
animal conflict in the country include: 
i.  Funds are provided under the National CAMPA for augmentation of fodder and 
water in forest areas for restricting wild animals to forest areas.  An amount of 
Rs. 47,872.31 crores has been provided to various States for  promoting 
afforestation and achieving green objectives of the country during 2019-2020. 
ii. Ministry provides financial assistance to States/UTs under the Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes of 'Development of Wildlife Habitats', ‘Project Tiger’ and 
‘Project Elep hant’ for  management of wildlife and its habitats in the country. 
The broad activities supported under these schemes include habitat 
enrichment, water augmentation. 
iii. The funds are also used for construction /erection of physical barriers such as 
solar powered electric fence, bio -fencing using cactus, boundary wall, animal 
proof trenches around forest, etc. 
iv. The financial support to the States/UTs also includes a component of 
compensation due to damage by wild animals. 
v.  Voluntary relocation of villa ges from the core area of Tiger Reserves, National 
Parks and Sanctuaries are also being funded under the Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme: ‘Integrated Development of Wildlife Habitats’ as proposed by the 
State Governments for avoiding conflict. 

                                                        [8 FEBRUARY, 2021]                                                                47 
 
 
vi. Periodic awar eness ca mpaigns to sensitize, guide and advise the general 
public on man -animal conflict, including dissemination of information through 
various forms of media. 
vii. Directions have been sent to all States/Union Territories for use of 
undergrounding of cab les upto 33 KV of electricity cables in forest areas and 
also maintaining transmission lines to avoid sagging.  
viii. Government of India has issued Standard Operating Procedures 
(SOPs)/guidelines to manage Human -Tiger/Human-Leopard /Human -
Elephant conflict. 
ix. Ministry, in the year 2018, has increased ex -gratia relief under the Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme in case of depredation by wild animals. 
x. Under the revamped operational guidelines of Pradhan Mantri Fasal  Bima 
Yojna (PMFBY), issued by the Government o f Indi a (e ffective from the year 
2020), States can provide add -on coverage for crop loss due to attack by wild 
animals. 
xi. To mitigate human wildlife conflict along linear infrastructures like rail tracks, 
roads/highways and power transmission lines passi ng thr ough the Protected 
Areas and other wildlife rich areas, the Standing Committee of National Board 
for Wildlife has recommended that all linear infrastructure development 
Agencies, should submit animal passage plans based on the guidelines 
prepared by Wildlife Institute of India.  
xii. The Ministry has approved a project for undertaking immuno -contraceptive 
measures for population management of wild animals.

Development of traditional arts 
*70. SHRI BR IJLAL: Will the Minister of MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM 
ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
(a)  the details of schemes in place for development of traditional arts of the country;  
(b)  whether any scheme is under consideration to identify and  develop local arts  of 
other States on the lines of ‘One District One Product’ scheme popularly known as 
ODOP being run by Government of Uttar Pradesh; and  
(c)  if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (SHRI NITIN 
JAIRAM GADKARI): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises is implementing a scheme 
titled ‘Scheme of Fund for Traditional Industries (SFURTI)’.  The main objective of the 
SFURTI s cheme is to organize  the traditional industries and artisans into clusters, 
including clusters of traditional arts, to make them competitive and provide long term 
sustainable employment.  
Under the scheme, two types of clusters are set up.  The maximum fin ancial 
assistance provided is Rs.  2.50 crore for a Regular Cluster (up to 500 artisans) and 

                                                        [8 FEBRUARY, 2021]                                                                59 
 
 
Rs. 5.00 crore for a Major Cluster (more than 500 artisans).  The assistance includes 
infrastructure development like setting up of Common Facility Centers, procure ment 
of new machineries, raw materials, along with training, exposure visits, etc. 
Till date, 335 clusters have been approved under the scheme and 82 clusters 
are functional. These clusters inc lude sectors like Khadi, Coir, Handloom, Traditional 
Dress Maki ng, Handicraft, Traditional Arts like – Kalamkari, Dokra art, Bamboo 
products, Food processing including honey, etc.  The list of these clusters is placed 
at Annexure. 
Besides this, Ministry of  Textiles implements schemes 
for development of traditional arts under ‘National Hand icraft Development 
Programme (NHDP)’ that has 7 components namely (i) Ambedkar Hastshilp Vikas 
Yojana (Base Line Survey & Mobilization of artisans), (ii) Design & Technolo gy Up 
gradation, (iii) Human Resource Development, (iv) Direct Benefit to Artisan, (v ) 
Infrastructure and Technology Support, (vi) Research and Development and (vii) 
Marketing Support & Services. In addition, Ministry of Textiles implements 
‘Comprehensive Handicrafts Cluster Development Scheme (CHCDS)’ that has two 
components namely Mega Cluster & Special Projects under Integrated Development 
and Promotion of Handicraft (IDPH). 
Ministry of Tourism under the Swadesh Darshan scheme provides financial 
assistance to the State Govt./UTs/Central Agencies for setting up proje cts as part of 
development of tourism infrastructure in the country.  Craft Haat/Craft Bazaar, Open 
Air Theatre/Amphi theatres, Souvenir Shops are set up under the scheme to help 
development of traditional arts in the country. 
Ministry of Minority Affairs is implementing a scheme titled USTTAD (Upgrading 
the Skills and Training in Traditional Arts/ Crafts for Development) that aims at 
capacity building and upgrading the traditional skills of maste r craftsmen/artisans; 
training of minority youths in various i dentified traditional arts/crafts; develop national 
and international market linkages and preservation of languishing arts/crafts. Hunar  
Haat has been implemented as a component of this scheme wh ich is an effective 
platform wherein opportunity is given to minority artisans/crafts men and culinary 
experts from across the country to showcase and market their finest handicraft and 
exquisitely crafted indigenous products. 23 Hunar  Haats have been organi zed since 
November, 2016 till December 2020 at different places.

MOTION OF THANKS ON THE PRESIDENT’S ADDRESS 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, the House has taken up the discussion on Motion 
of Thanks on the President’s Address, and we have spent around fifteen hours and 
more than fifty hon. Members from different political parties have tak en part in the 
discussion. Now, it is the time for conclusion, and the reply is going to be given by 
the hon. Prime Minister. So, I call upon hon. Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Bhai Modi 
to reply. 
DR. SANTANU SEN (West Bengal): Sir, All India Trinamool Congress is walking out. 
SHRI MD. NADIMUL HAQUE (West Bengal): Sir, we are walking out. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: He has already said it. He is your leader, follow the leader. Thank 
you. 
(At this stage, some hon. Members left the Chamber) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: This is not a matter of joking. If they want to walk out, they have the 
right. Walk out or talk out is the way out, not the wash out or all out. I am happy. 
Now, hon. Prime Minister will reply to Motion of Thanks on the President’s Address. 
THE PRIME MINISTER (SHRI NARENDRA  MODI): Honourable  Chairman Sir , the 
whole world is facing various challenges these days. Hardly anyone would have 
thought that the mankind would have to pass through such difficult tim es. Amid such 
challenges, our honourable President addressed the Joint Sitting of the Parliament at 
the beginning of this decade which in itself has instilled a new hope, new zeal and 
new confidence to the world full of challenges. The President's address has been a 
guiding principle for 'self -reliant India' and paved the way  to be followed for the 
decade. Honourable Chairman, Sir, today, I rise here among all of you to express my 
gratitude from the bottom of my heart to the honourable President. 
 More than 50 honourable Members expressed their valuable views on the 
various aspects for 13 to 14 hours in Raj ya Sabha. Therefore, I express my heartfelt 
gratitude towards all the honourable Members for enriching this debate. It would have 

84 [RAJYA SABHA] 
 
been better if all the Me mbers were present during the President's Address which 
would have fur ther dignified our democracy an d would also give no occasion to 
complain to anyone that we could not listen to the  President's Address. But the 
content of the President's address was so effective that despite its boycott, the 
honourable Members spoke about  it at length. It was the stren gth of the speech, the 
thoughts and the ideals itself that the message was conveyed although they did not 
listen to it. Hence, in my view the speech has immense value. 
 Honourable Chairman Sir, as I said that this was the fir st address of this 
decade deliv ered by the honourable President amid various challenges but at the 
same time it is also right that, today, when we look at the entire world and the young 
minds of India, it seems like India is truly the land of opportunities. Many opportunities 
are awaiting us. That is why a country which is young, zealous and striving to fulfil its 
various dreams with determination can never afford to ignore these  opportunities. 
This is also an inspiring opportunity for all of us that we are  entering the 75 th year of 
Independence. No matter wherever we are or whatever we are, as the sons and 
daughters of Mother India, we all should celebrate this 75thanniversary of 
Independence as a festival of inspiration. We all should have the passion to 
accomplish something in order to prepare the country for the ensuing years. We 
should keep dreaming about how further we are going to take the country by the time 
it celebrates the centenary of its independence in 2047. 
 Sir, today, entire world is looking towards India. While on one han d there are 
many expectations from India, at the same time people also have a  belief that if India 
accomplishes something, number of problems would be resolv ed. This is the 
increasing faith that the world today has in India. 
 Honourable Chairman Sir, as I am  discussing the opportunities, I would like to 
quote a poem by the great poet Shri Maithilisharan Gupta ji. Gupta ji said:- 
"Avasar tere liye khada hai, 
Fir bhi tu chup chap pada hai. 
Tera karmshetra bada hai, 
Pal pal hai anmol. 
Are Bharat! Uth, aankhein khol." 
 But I was thinking what he would write if he had to write during the period of 
beginning of 21st century. I assume that he would write:-

"Avasar tere liye khada hai, 
Tu atamavishwas se bhara pada hai. 
Hath badha, har bandish ko tod, 
Are Bharat! Atamnirbharta ke path par daud." 
 Honourable Chairman Sir, the kind of situations arose in the world during 
Corona made it impossible for everyone to help someone. A coun try could not help 
another country. A state could not he lp another state. Even a family mem ber could 
not help another member of his own family. This was the situation due to 
Coronavirus. The world expressed many doubts about India. The world was worried if 
India would not be able to take care of itself in this Coronavirus pandemic, not only 
India, the whole mankind will be facing a huge crisis. T his doubt was expressed by 
everyone. Billions of people will be stuck. Millions of people will die. A lot of fear 
mongering was also witnessed here. Why did it happen? I t is not my question as no 
one had the idea about, what an unknown enemy can do. Everyone evaluated it in his 
own way. But in order to protest its citizens, India fought with an unknown enemy for 
which there was no known pattern or protocol as to how to de al with it. Nothing was 
known. Everyone had to move in a new way with a new thinking. Some scholarly and 
able persons might have a different opinion but as it was an unknown enemy, we had 
to find the way, m ake the way and save the people as well. This coun try tried to do 
everything to the b est of its wisdom, strength and ability that the almighty bestowed 
at that time and worked hard to save itself. Today, the world is really proud of India 
for it has played a vital role in saving the mankind in this world.  The credit of winning 
this fight does not go to just one person or one Government but to entire nation. What 
do we lose by feeling proud of it or explaining it to the world with confidence? This 
country has done it and poorest of the poor of this country has contributed to it. You 
would have seen it on social media at that time that even an old lady sitting on the 
footpath at her small hut had lit a lamp outside her hut to pray for the wellbeing of 
India. We are making fun of it and such feelings. Someone who did not even visit a 
school eve r had tried to help with a feeling that whatever the way I can serve the 
nation, I shall do it even by lighting a lamp. This feeling awakened a collective strength 
in the country and displayed her power and ability. But p eople are enjoying making 
fun of this too. Today, there are so many issues to protest for. And we should protest 
too but we should not engage in such activities which weaken the morale and 
underestimates th e potential of the country. This can never be bene ficial. You can 
imagine how our corona warriors and frontline workers worked. Doing one's duty and 
fulfilling one's responsibilities during such times whe n corona might come from

anywhere is not an ordinary thing. We should be proud of them and respect the m. It

not to criticize anybody but when we look into the past as we had lived through those

different places in Jammu and Kashmir, meeting people, inaugu rating developmental 
activities, taking petitions, disseminating message of Narendra Modi, development 
message of Central Government. Similarly, in th e name of 'Saubhagya', there i s 
'Prime Minister' 'Ujjwala Yojana', 'Ujala Yojana', and 'Swachh Bharat' sch eme.

districts are in huge debts and have mortgaged their lands , sold all their jewels, 
drained their savings and virtually standing on streets.

closed mills as nationalised banks have priority over these debts and they have 
invoked the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) by initiating insolvency 
proceedings.  The National Cooperative Sugar Mill has not paid State Advisory Price 
on sugar cane for a period of two years.

Best practices for maintaining Air Quality Index 
 
*62. SHRI RAJMANI PATEL: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND 
CLIMATE CHANGE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware that the State of Punjab recorded a moderate Air 
Quality Index (AQI) in September- October 2020 despite 11,000 stubble 
burning cases, whereas Delhi’s AQI was poor during the same period; 
(b) whether Government has identified causes for this difference between the two 
region's AQI; 
(c) if so, the details thereof, and if not, the reasons therefor; 
[8 February, 2021]
27

(d) whether Government has identified good practices of the State Government of 
Punjab to reduce air pollution; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof, and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND CLIMATE CHANGE (SHRI PRAKASH 
JAVADEKAR): (a) to (e) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
 
Statement 
 
(a) to (e) Considering the importance of the clean air, Government has launched Air 
Quality Index (AQI) in the year 2015. 
 
Air Quality Index (AQI) provides air pollution status of an area or city but not that of 
any State. AQI of a city depends on multiple factors, which include meteorology, 
geography, local sources such as vehicles, industries, etc. and contribution from 
other regional sources. 
Delhi with higher population, number of vehicles, emission from various other lo cal 
sources as well as contribution of regional sources such as stubble burning (during 
October, November), dust in summer has higher air pollution levels compared to 
many of the adjoining cities including cities of Punjab.  
 
With low winds, low temperatures and limited mixing area available for dilution, the 
pollution levels in Delhi are higher during winter. In October and November, wind 
blows from Punjab towards Delhi. This brings pollution due to stubble burning towards 
Delhi and adds to Delhi’s pollution.  
 
It is observed that meteorology plays very important role in air pollution. Other 
metropolitan cities like Chennai, Bengaluru and Mumbai have similar or more pollution 
sources as Delhi. But, air quality in these cities is far better than Delhi due to high 
winds and mixing zone and other meteorological factors.  
 
With many actions taken by the Government such as introduction of BS-VI, expansion 
of Metro, operationalization of Eastern and Western peripheral expressways, shifting 
of industries to PNG, waste processing plants, online round the clock monitoring of 
red category industries, etc. Air quality has improved significantly in Delhi.  Details are 
annexed.

Punjab has reported that actions such as mandatory use of Super Straw Management 
System with Combine Harvester, deployment of district level teams to take stric t

CENTRAL GOVERNMENT INITIATIVES TO COMBAT AIR POLLUTION IN DELHI- 
NCR 
 
1. ACTIONS TO CONTROL VEHICLE POLLUTION 
 
Introduction of BS-IV and BS-VI Fuel and Emission Norms  
 BS IV fuel and vehicle emission norms were introduced in April 2017 in the entire 
country. BS VI fuel was introduced in Delhi from April 2018, in NCR from October 
2019 and in entire country by April 2020. 
 80% reduction in Particulate Matter emissions and 30% reduction in Nitrogen 
Oxides emissions in BS IV heavy duty diesel vehicles compared with BS III norms. 
 Leapfrogging to BS VI norms is likely to reduce 50% Particulate Matter emissions 
and 88.5% Nitrogen Oxide emissions in comparison to BS IV norms. 
Improvement also in other pollutants and type of vehicles.  
 Nearly ₹60,000 Cr were spent on switching over to BS VI fuels. 
 
Eastern and Western Peripheral Expressways (EPE and WPE) 
 EPE and WPE work completed at cost of about ₹17000 Cr and opened for public 
in May 2018 and November 2018, respectively.  
 30000 to 40000 good vehicles not destined for Delhi ar e diverted away from 
national capital due to WPE and EPE. This helps in reduction traffic congestion 
and pollution caused due to non- destined vehicles which earlier used to pass 
through Delhi. 
Implementation of RFID system at all 13 entry points of Delhi

 RFID (radio -frequency identity) system implemented by South Delhi Municipal 
Corporation (SDMC) for collection of toll and Environment Compensation 
Charges from commercial vehicles entering Delhi. 
 Cost ₹120 Cr for over the period of next five years (Design, Built, Finance, 
Operate and Transfer) basis. 
 Strict enforcement of Environmental Compensation Charges on Delhi -bound 
trucks helps in control on numbers, including enforcement to check and divert all 
non-Delhi bound truck traffic and age limit (as stipulate d by Hon’ble Supreme 
Court). 
Motor Vehicle Act 2019: Increase in penalty for violation of PUC norms 
 With recent amendment in the Motor Vehicle Act and increase in fine from ₹1000/- 
to ₹10000/-for not having PUC certificate, compliance has increased.  Due t o 
this, average number of daily PUC certificates issued has increased from 10,000 -
12,000 to 40000-45000. 
 
 PUC norms compliance and traffic discipline will help in reduction in vehicular 
pollution in Delhi-NCR, which has a major contribution to pollution levels in Delhi-
NCR. 
Installation of Vapour Recovery Systems in more than 3000 petrol pumps in NCR is 
under implementation. 
Delhi Metro Network Augmentation 
 Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) network now covers about 389 Km with 
285 stations, reaching Delhi-Noida-Greater Noida-Ghaziabad in UP and Gurgaon 
to Ballabhgarh in Haryana. It today has over 300 train sets of four, six and eight 
coaches. 
 Metro network expansion plays an important role in pollution reduction in Delhi -
NCR as it shifts more and more private vehicles user to public transport, thus, 
minimizing use of individual cars as well as by reducing traffic congestion.  
 Environmental friendly Metro at cost of more than ₹70,000 Cr is used by over 30 
lakhs people every day and because of this 4,00,000  vehicles are avoided on 
roads, thereby, reducing pollution.

Adoption and Manufacture of (Hybrid &) Electric Vehicles in India (FAME India) 
scheme. Commencing from 1

(a) whether Government is aware of the fact that the population of various wild 
species have multiplied during the last few years and that they are posing danger 
by encroaching into agriculture fields and nearby human habitations, near forest

(b) if so, the measures taken by Government to control the human -animal conflict 
in the country? 
 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND CLIMATE CHANGE (SHRI PRAKASH 
JAVADEKAR): (a) and (b) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
  
Statement 
 
46
[RAJYA SABHA]

(a) and (b) As a result of concerted efforts made for protection and 
conservation of wildlife, the population of several wildlife species like Tigers, 
Elephants, Asiatic Lion, Rhino etc. in the country has increased. There are 
reports of wild animals moving out of the forests leading to human wildlife 
conflict situations. 
 
The management of wildlife is primarily the responsibility of the concerned 
States/Union Territories.  
The important steps taken by Government of India to manage and mitigate 
human-animal conflict in the country include: 
i.  Funds are provided under the National CAMPA for augmentation of 
fodder and water in forest areas for restricting wild animals to forest areas.  An 
amount of Rs. 47,872.31 Crores has been provided to various States for 
promoting afforestation and achieving green objectives of the country during 
2019-2020. 
ii. Ministry provides financial assistance to States/UTs under the Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes of 'Development of Wildlife Habitats', ‘Project Tiger’ and 
‘Project Elephant’ for management of wildlife and its habitats in the country. 
The broad activities supported under these schem es include habitat 
enrichment, water augmentation. 
iii. The funds are also used for construction /erection of physical barriers 
such as solar powered electric fence, bio-fencing using cactus, boundary wall, 
animal proof trenches around forest, etc. 
iv. The financial support to the States/UTs also includes a component of 
compensation due to damage by wild animals. 
v.  Voluntary relocation of villages from the core area of Tiger Reserves, 
National Parks and Sanctuaries are also being funded under the Centrall y 
Sponsored Scheme: ‘Integrated Development of Wildlife Habitats’ as proposed 
by the State Governments for avoiding conflict. 
vi. Periodic awareness campaigns to sensitize, guide and advise the 
general public on man -animal conflict, including dissemination  of information 
through various forms of media. 
vii. Directions have been sent to all States/Union Territories for use of 
undergrounding of cables upto 33 KV of electricity cables  in forest areas and 
also maintaining transmission lines to avoid sagging.

viii. Government of India has issued Standard Operating Procedures 
(SOPs)/guidelines to manage Human -Tiger/Human-Leopard /Human -
Elephant conflict. 
ix. Ministry, in the year 2018, has increased ex -gratia relief under the 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme in case of depredation by wild animals. 
x. Under the revamped operational guidelines of Pradhan Mantri Fasal 
Bima Yojna (PMFBY), issued by the Government of India (effective from the 
year 2020), States can provide  add -on  coverage for crop loss due to attack 
by wild animals. 
xi. To mitigate human wildlife conflict along linear infrastructures like rail 
tracks, roads/highways and power transmission lines passing through the 
Protected Areas and other wildlife rich areas, the Standing Committee of 
National Board for Wildlife has recommended that all linear infrastructure 
development Agencies, should submit animal passage plans based on the 
guidelines prepared by Wildlife Institute of India.  
xii. The Ministry has approved a project for undertaking immuno -
contraceptive measures for population management of wild animals.

THE MINISTER OF JAL SHAKTI (SHRI GAJENDRA SINGH SHEKHAWAT): (a) to 
(d)    A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
 
 
 
 
Statement 
 
(a)  to (d)   Hon’ble Chief Minister, Government of Andhra Pradesh (GoAP), vide 
letter dated 05.02.2020, has inter -alia requested for intervention of Government of 
India to streamline the procedure for reimbursement of project cost to GoAP in 
respect of Polavaram Irrigation Project (PIP). 
  Government of India has been reimbursing the expenditure on Irrigation 
component of the PIP with effect from 01.04.2014, upon receipt of verified bills and 
recommendations from the Polavaram Project Authority (PPA) and Central Water 
Commission (CWC), with the approval of Ministry of Finance (MoF). 
  Funds are being provided for PIP through Extra Budgetary Resources (EBR) 
from NABARD under Long Term Irrigation Fund (LTIF), after seeking specific approval 
from MoF.   
Further, NABARD raises the funds from the market once requirement of requisite 
amounts is conveyed to them by this Ministry. NABARD normally requires about two 
to three weeks to arrange funds from market (depending upon market conditions) 
and transfer to National Water Development Agency (NWDA). Thereafter, the funds 
are transferred to the GoAP promptly by PPA, normally within one or two working 
days. 
 Response along above lines, was duly conveyed to the Hon’ble CM, GoAP, vide 
letter dated 06
th July 2020.

†*70. SHRI BRIJLAL: Will the Minister of MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM 
ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
(a)  the details of schemes in place for development of traditional arts of the country;  
(b)  whether any scheme is under consideration to identify and develop local arts of 
other States on the lines of ‘One District One Product’ scheme popularly known as 
ODOP being run by Government of Uttar Pradesh; and  
(c)  if so, the details thereof? 
 
THE MINISTER OF MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (SHRI NITIN 
JAIRAM GADKARI): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House.

Statement 
 
(a) Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises is implementing a scheme 
titled ‘Scheme of Fund for Traditional Industries (SFURTI)’.  The main objective of the 
SFURTI scheme is to organize the traditional industries and artisans into clusters, 
including clusters of traditional arts, to make them competitive and provide long term 
sustainable employment.  
Under the scheme, two types of clusters are set up.  The maximum financial 
assistance provided is Rs.2.50 crore for a Regular Cluster (up to 500 artisans) and 
Rs.5.00 crore for a Major Cluster (more than 500 artisans).  The assistance includes 
infrastructure development like setting up of Common Facility Centers, procurement 
of new machineries, raw materials, along with training, exposure visits, etc. 
Till date, 335 clusters have been approved under the scheme and 82 clusters 
are functional. These clusters include sectors like Khadi, Coir, Handloom, Traditional 
Dress Making, Handicraft, Hraditional Arts like – Kalamkari, Dokra art, Bamboo 
products, Food proce ssing including honey, etc.  The list of these clusters is placed 
at Annexure.  
Besides this, Ministry of Textiles implements schemes 
for development of traditional arts under ‘National Handicraft Development 
Programme (NHDP)’ that has 7 components namely (i) Ambedkar Hastshilp Vikas 
Yojana (Base Line Survey & Mobilization of artisans), (ii) Design & Technology Up 
gradation, (iii) Human Resource Development, (iv) Direct Benefit to Artisan, (v) 
Infrastructure and Technology Support, (vi) Research and Develop ment and (vii) 
Marketing Support & Services. In addition, Ministry of Textiles implements 
‘Comprehensive Handicrafts Cluster Development Scheme (CHCDS)’ that has two 
components namely Mega Cluster & Special Projects under Integrated Development 
and Promotion of Handicraft (IDPH). 
Ministry of Tourism under the Swadesh Darshan scheme provides financial 
assistance to the State Govt./UTs/Central Agencies for setting up projects as part of 
development of tourism infrastructure in the country.   Craft Haat/Craft Bazaar, Open 
Air Theatre/Amphi theatres, Souvenir Shops are set up under the scheme to help 
development of traditional arts in the country. 
Ministry of Minority Affairs is implementing a scheme titled  USTTAD  
(Upgrading the Skills and Training in Tradition al Arts/ Crafts for Development) that 
aims at capacity building and upgrading the traditional skills of master 
craftsmen/artisans; training of minority youths in various identified traditional 
arts/crafts; develop national and international market linkages  and preservation of

languishing arts/crafts. Hunar Haat has been implemented as a component of this 
scheme which is an effective platform wherein opportunity is given to minority 
artisans/craftsmen and culinary experts from across the country to showcase and 
market their finest handicraft and exquisitely crafted indigenous products. 23 Hunar 
Haats have been organized since November, 2016 till December 2020 at different 
places. 
 Ministry of Rural Development under Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana-National 
Rural L ivelihood Mission (DAY -NRLM) is implementing a scheme for promoting 
handloom and handicraft artisanal clusters. The scheme is being implemented in 13 
States (Assam, Bihar, Chattisgarh, Gujarat, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Madhya 
Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and West 
Bengal). 
 
(b) and (c) No, sir.

cooking and drinking purposes. To expedite the implementation of Jal Jeevan Mission,
regular review meetings are held and field visits along with follow-up with State
Governments.

water supply to every household by 2022, whereas Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Nagaland 
and Tripura by 2023 and Assam by 2024.

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARAS (a) TO (e) OF THE RAJYA 
SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 62 DUE FOR REPLY ON 08.02.2021 REGRADING 
BEST PRACTICES FOR MAINTAINING AIR QUALITY INDEX RAISED BY SHRI 
RAJMANI PATEL, HON’BLE MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT 
 
(a) to (e) 
Considering the importance of the clean air, Government has launched Air Quality Index 
(AQI) in the year 2015. 
 
Air Quality Index (AQI) provides air pollution status of an area or city but not that of any 
State. AQI of a city depends on multiple factors, which include meteorology, geography, 
local sources such as vehicles, industries, etc. and contribution from other regional 
sources. 
Delhi with higher population, number of vehicles, emission from various other local 
sources as well as contribution of regional sources such as stubble burning (during 
October, November), dust in summer has higher air pollution levels compared to many of 
the adjoining cities including cities of Punjab.  
 
With low winds, low temperatures and limited mixing area available for dilution, the 
pollution levels in Delhi are higher during winter. In October and November, wind blows 
from Punjab towards Delhi. This brings pollution due to stubble burning towards Delhi 
and adds to Delhi’s pollution.  
 
It is observed that meteorology plays very important role in air pollution. Other 
metropolitan cities like Chennai, Bengaluru and Mumbai have similar or more pollution 
sources as Delhi. But, air quality in these cities is far better than Delhi due to high winds 
and mixing zone and other meteorological factors.  
 
With many actions taken by the Government such as introduction of BS-VI, expansion of 
Metro, operationalization of Eastern and Western peripheral expressways, shifting of 
industries to PNG, waste processing plants, online round the clock monitoring of red 
category industries, etc. Air quality has improved significantly in Delhi.  Details are 
annexed. 
 
The ‘Good’, ‘Satisfactory’ and ‘Moderate’ days increased to 182 in 2019 in comparison to 
108 in 2016 whereas, number of ‘Poor’, ‘Very Poor’ and ‘Severe’ reduced from 246 in 
2016 to 183 in 2019.  
 
Punjab has reported that actions such as mandatory use of Super Straw Management 
System with Combine Harvester, deployment of district level teams to take strict actions 
against defaulters, putting up biomass power plants, public awareness campaigns, etc. 
were taken. However, the incidences of stubble burning reported in 2020 (76,590) has 
increased as compared to last year (52,991 cases).

CENTRAL GOVERNMENT INITIATIVES TO COMBAT AIR POLLUTION IN 
DELHI- NCR 
 
1. ACTIONS TO CONTROL VEHICLE POLLUTION 
 
Introduction of BS-IV and BS-VI Fuel and Emission Norms  
 BS IV fuel and vehicle emission norms were introduced in April 2017 in the entire 
country. BS VI fuel was introduced in Delhi from April 2018, in NCR from October 2019 
and in entire country by April 2020. 
 80% reduction in Particulate Matter emissions and 30% reduction in Nitrogen Oxides 
emissions in BS IV heavy duty diesel vehicles compared with BS III norms. 
 Leapfrogging to BS VI norms is likely to reduce 50% Particulate Matter emissions and 
88.5% Nitrogen Oxide emissions in comparison to BS IV norms. Improvement also in 
other pollutants and type of vehicles.  
 Nearly ₹60,000 Cr were spent on switching over to BS VI fuels. 
 
Eastern and Western Peripheral Expressways (EPE and WPE) 
 EPE and WPE work completed at cost of about ₹17000 Cr and opened for public in May 
2018 and November 2018, respectively.  
 30000 to 40000 good vehicles not destined for Delhi are diverted away from national 
capital due to WPE and EPE. This helps in reduction traffic congestion and pollution 
caused due to non-destined vehicles which earlier used to pass through Delhi. 
Implementation of RFID system at all 13 entry points of Delhi 
 RFID (radio-frequency identity) system implemented by South Delhi Municipal 
Corporation (SDMC) for collection of toll and Environment Compensation Charges from 
commercial vehicles entering Delhi. 
 Cost ₹120 Cr for over the period of next five years (Design, Built, Finance, Operate and 
Transfer) basis. 
 Strict enforcement of Environmental Compensation Charges on Delhi-bound trucks 
helps in control on numbers, including enforcement to check and divert all non-Delhi 
bound truck traffic and age limit (as stipulated by Hon’ble Supreme Court). 
Motor Vehicle Act 2019: Increase in penalty for violation of PUC norms 
 
 With recent amendment in the Motor Vehicle Act and increase in fine from ₹1000/- to 
₹10000/-for not having PUC certificate, compliance has increased.  Du e to this, average 
number of daily PUC certificates issued has increased from 10,000-12,000 to 40000-
45000. 
 
 PUC norms compliance and traffic discipline will help in reduction in vehicular pollution 
in Delhi-NCR, which has a major contribution to pollution levels in Delhi-NCR. 
 
Installation of Vapour Recovery Systems in more than 3000 petrol pumps in NCR is under 
implementation. 
Delhi Metro Network Augmentation 
 Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) network now covers about 389 Km with 285 
stations, reaching Delhi-Noida-Greater Noida-Ghaziabad in UP and Gurgaon to 
Ballabhgarh in Haryana. It today has over 300 train sets of four, six and eight coaches. 
9

 Metro network expansion plays an important role in pollution reduction in Delhi-NCR as 
it shifts more and more private vehicles user to public transport, thus, minimizing use of 
individual cars as well as by reducing traffic congestion.  
 Environmental friendly Metro at cost of more than ₹70,000 Cr is used by over 30 lakhs 
people every day and because of this 4,00,000 vehicles are avoided on roads, thereby, 
reducing pollution.  
E-mobility Initiatives 
 Department of Heavy Industry is providing subsidy on e-vehicles under Faster Adoption 
and Manufacture of (Hybrid &) Electric Vehicles in India (FAME India) scheme. 
Commencing from 1st April 2019, Phase-II of FAME Scheme has been approved with an 
outlay of Rs. 10,000 Crore for a period of 3 years. 48145 electric vehicles
 have been sold 
in the country under FAME-II scheme. 
 Setting up of public charging stations (PCS) had been de-licensed and any 
individual/entity is free to set up PCS. EESL has installed more than 70 Public charging 
stations in Delhi NCR.  
 States advised to exempt road tax on e-vehicles thereby reducing cost of purchase of 
ecofriendly vehicles. 
2. ACTIONS TO CONTROL ROAD AND CONSTRUCTION & DEMOLITION 
DUST 
 Construction & Demolition (C & D) Waste Management Rules were notified in 2016  
 
3. ACTIONS FOR C&D WASTE PROCESSING IN DELHI 
 
 03 C & D Waste Processing Plants (Jahangirpuri, Shastri Park and Ranikhera) with total 
capacity of 2650 TPD are operational in Delhi. 
 04 new plants (Baba Hardis nagar, Siraspur, New Ranikhera, Bakkarwala) are being 
established to increase the processing capacity by 3000TPD. 
 At present, 57 lakhMT C&D waste is being processed, with an off-take of 8,83,028 MT. 
 76 mechanized road sweeping machines (number of machines as in September 2019: 
Delhi - 60, Ghaziabad - 06, Greater Noida - 06, Noida – 04) and 502 water sprinklers to 
various municipal corporations with support ₹280 Cr. 
 
4. ACTIONS TO CONTROL INDUSTRIAL EMISSIONS 
 
 Thermal Power Plants 
- Closure of Badarpur Thermal Plant of NTPC led to estimated reduction of 8 tons of 
particulate matter, 44.7 tons  of Sulphur dioxide (SO 2) and 128.4 tons of Oxides of 
Nitrogen (NOx) emissions per day 
- Implementation of new emission norms in thermal power plants will lead to 
reduction in emission of particulate matter by 92 tons , Sulphur dioxide (SO 2) by 
898tons and Oxides of Nitrogen (NOx) by 474 tons per day in NCR Delhi.  
 SO2 and NOx standards for industrial boilers and Five Industrial Sectors (Ceramic, 
Foundry, Glass, Lime Kiln & Reheating Furnace) introduced. Out of 1511 operational 
industries in these sectors in Delhi-NCR, 1388 units have reported compliance with the 
norms. 
 It is estimated that ban on use of petcoke in NCR has led to 48% reduction in total PM 
emission as compared to using Furnace Oil.   
 Out of 5147 industrial units in Delhi NCR,3074 have shifted to PNG. 
 Out of 621 Red Category Air Polluting Units in Delhi NCR, OCEMS have been installed 
and connected to CPCB server by 563 units.

 Solid Waste Management Rules have been revamped in 2016 
 Out of 10470 TPD municipal solid waste generated in Delhi, About 10466 TPD waste

- 100 TPD Bio methanation plant for treating cattle dung at Ghazipur has been

 Bio mining of three dumpsites at Bhalsawa, Okhla and Ghazipur. Work for bio 
mining has been initiated at these three sites. 
 
6. MEASURES TO CONTROL OF STUBBLE BURNING 
 In- situ Management of Crop Residue:  A Central sector scheme launched by 
Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare in 2018, ‘ Promotion of Agricultural 
Mechanization for in-situ Management of Crop Residue in Punjab, Haryana and 
Uttar Pradesh and NCT of Delhi’  to address air pollution due to stubble burning.  
The Scheme has been approved for continuation during 2020-21 with an outlay of Rs. 
600 crores. 
 70,449 machines have been distributed so far along with establishment of28, 907 
Custom Hiring Centres (CHCs) in Punjab, Haryana, U. P. and Delhi 
 In terms of Active Fire Events, stubble burning incidents has reduced by 25% (1652 
AFEs) in comparison to 2019 in Haryana.

As informed by the Government of West Bengal, thepopulation of Red 
Panda was estimated to be 32 in Neora Valley National Park and 38 in 
Singalila National Park in the year 2012.Estimates indicate that the 
numbers of Red Panda after 2012 are on the rise. 
Red Panda are foundin the temperate montane forests in the eastern 
Himalayas. In India, Red Pandas are found in States of Sikkim, 
Arunachal Pradesh, West Bengal and Meghalaya. T hey are arboreal 
species and depend on bamboo for their survival. 
As informed by the Government of West Bengal  and Wildlife Crime 
Control Bureau,no case of Red Panda poaching or illegal trade of its body 
parts has been reported in West Bengal.  
Indian Pangolins, also known as scaly ant eaters, live in burrows  and are 
found in large numbers in tropical forests as well as open land, grasslands 
and degraded habitatsthrough out the country except North Eastern 
States.  Population assessment of Indian Pangolins is not carried out.

he measures taken by the Government to control illegal poaching and 
illegal trafficking of wild animals including Pangolins and Red 
Pandasinclude: 
i. In the year 2018, the Standing Committee of National Board for
Wildlife approved the inclusion of Red Panda as one of the
species under ‘Recovery Programme for Critically Endangered
Species’ for financial assistance under the Centrally Sponsored
Scheme: ‘Development of Wildlife Habitats’.
ii. The Government of India is supporting a project: ‘ Red Panda
augmentation Programme in Singalila National Park and Neora
Valley National Park in West Bengal ’, submitted by Government
of West Bengal which, inter alia, includes conservation breeding
of Red Panda and re-stocking of the population of Red Panda in
24

the wild. Financial support to the tune of Rs. 2.446 Crores has 
been sanctioned to West Bengal under this project. 
 
iii.  Funds are provided by the Government of India  under 
‘Integrated Development of Wildlife Habitats’ for  habitat 
enrichment  including maintenance of grasslands, which, inter-
alia, helps in conservation of Indian Pangolin. 
 
iv. Both Indian Pangolin and Red Panda are listed in Schedule – I of 
Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972, giving them the highest status 
of protection in the country. 
 
v. Wildlife Crime Control Bureaugathers intelligence about 
poaching and unlawful trade in wild animals and animal articles 
and is responsible for inter-state and trans-boundary coordination 
in enforcement of wildlife laws.Wildlife Crime Control Bureau 
has coordinated species specific operation named LESKNOW 
towards control of poaching and illegal trade of lesser known 
wild animals including Pangolins.  Wildlife Crime Control 
Bureau has regularly participated in global operations such as 
operation THUNDERBALL envisaged by INTERPOL’s 
Wildlife working group for prevention of poaching and illegal 
trade of wildlife and their parts. 
 
 
(e) and (f) India is a member of South Asian Wildlife Enforcement Network and is 
also one of the collaborating nations with INTERPOL, which provide 
platform for cross border co-ordination among countries for sharing 
information and enforcement actions against transboundary wildlife 
crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking.

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (a) AND (b) OF THE RAJYA 
SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. *66 REGARDING “HUMAN-ANIMAL CONFLICT 
IN THE COUNTRY” BY DR. BANDA PRAKASH DUE FOR REPLY ON 08.02.2021. 
 
 
(a)  and (b) 
 
As a result of concerted efforts made for protection and conservation of wildlife, 
the population of several wildlife species like Tigers, Elephants, Asiatic Lion, 
Rhino etc. in the country has increased. There are reports of wild animals moving 
out of the forests leading to human wildlife conflict situations. 
 
The management of wildlife is primarily the responsibility of the concerned 
States/Union Territories.  
 
The important steps taken by Government of India to manage and mitigate human-
animal conflict in the country include: 
 
i.  Funds are provided under the National CAMPA for augmentation of fodder and 
water  in forest areas for restricting wild animals to forest areas.  An amount of  
Rs. 47,872.31 Crores has been provided to various States for promoting 
afforestation and achieving green objectives of the country during 2019-2020. 
 
ii. Ministry provides financial assistance to States/UTs under the Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes of 'Development of Wildlife Habitats', ‘Project Tiger’ 
and ‘Project Elephant’ for management of wildlife and its habitats in the 
country. The broad activities supported under these schemes include habitat 
enrichment,water augmentation. 
 
iii. The funds are also used for construction /erection of physical barriers such as 
solar powered electric fence, bio-fencing using cactus, boundary wall, animal 
proof trenches around forest, etc. 
 
iv. The financial support to the States/UTs also includes a component of 
compensation due to damage by wild animals. 
 
v.  Voluntary relocation of villages from the core area of Tiger Reserves, National 
Parks and Sanctuaries are also being funded under the Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme: ‘Integrated Development of Wildlife Habitats’ as proposed by the 
State Governments for avoiding conflict. 
 
vi. Periodic awareness campaigns to sensitize, guide and advise the general public 
on man-animal conflict, including dissemination of information through various 
forms of media. 
 
vii. Directions have been sent to all States/Union Territories for use of 
undergrounding of cables upto 33 KV of electricity cables  in forest areas and 
also maintaining transmission lines to avoid sagging.  
 
55

 
viii. Government of India has issued Standard Operating Procedures 
(SOPs)/guidelines to manage Human-Tiger/Human-Leopard /Human-Elephant 
conflict. 
 
 
ix. Ministry, in the year 2018, has increased ex-gratia relief under the Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme in case of depredation by wild animals. 
 
x. Under the revamped operational guidelines of Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima 
Yojna (PMFBY), issued by the Government of India (effective from the year 
2020), States can provide  add-on  coverage for crop loss due to attack by wild 
animals. 
 
xi. To mitigate human wildlife conflict along linear infrastructures like rail tracks, 
roads/highways and power transmission lines passing through the Protected 
Areas and other wildlife rich areas, the Standing Committee of National Board 
for Wildlife has recommended that all linear infrastructure development 
Agencies, should submit animal passage plans based on the guidelines prepared 
by Wildlife Institute of India.  
 
 
xii. The Ministry has approved a project for undertaking immuno-contraceptive 
measures for population management of wild animals.

(a) to (d) Hon’ble Chief Minister, Government of Andhra Pradesh (GoAP), vide letter dated
05.02.2020, has inter-alia requested for intervention of Government of India to streamline the procedure
for reimbursement of project cost to GoAP in respect of Polavaram Irrigation Project (PIP).
Government of In dia has been reimbursing the expenditure on Irrigation component of the PIP
with effect from 01.04.2014, upon receipt of verified bills and recommendations from the Polavaram
Project Authority (PPA) and Central Water Commission (CWC), with the approval of Ministry of
Finance (MoF).
Funds are being provided for PIP through Extra Budgetary Resources (EBR) from NABARD
under Long Term Irrigation Fund (LTIF), after seeking specific approval from MoF.
Further, NABARD raises the funds from the market once re quirement of requisite amounts is
conveyed to them by this Ministry. NABARD normally requires about two to three weeks to arrange
funds from market (depending upon market conditions) and transfer to National Water Development
Agency (NWDA). Thereafter, the funds are transferred to the GoAP promptly by PPA, normally within
one or two working days.
Response along above lines, was duly conveyed to the Hon’ble CM, GoAP, vide letter dated 06 th
July 2020.

SABHA STARRED QUESTION No.*70 FOR ANSWER ON 08.02.2021 
 
(a): Ministry of Micro, 
Small and Medium Enterprises is implementing a scheme titled 
‘Scheme of Fund for Traditional Industries (SFURTI)’.  The main objective of the SFURTI 
scheme is to organize the traditional industries and artisans into clusters, including clusters of 
traditional arts, to make them competitive and provide long term sustainable employment.  
 
Under the scheme, two types of clusters are set up.  The maximum financial assistance 
provided is Rs.2.50 crore for a Regular Cluster (up to 500 artisans) and Rs.5.00 crore for a Major 
Cluster (more than 500 artisans).  The assistance includes infrastructure development like setting 
up of Common Facility Centers, procurement of new machineries, raw materials, along with 
training, exposure visits, etc. 
 
Till date, 335 clusters have been approved under the scheme and 82 clusters are 
functional. These clusters include sectors like Khadi, Coir, Handloom, Traditional Dress 
Making, Handicraft, Hraditional Arts like – Kalamkari, Dokra art, Bamboo products, Food 
processing including honey, etc.  The list of these clusters is placed at Annexure.  
 
Besides this, Ministry of Textiles implements schemes 
for development of traditional arts under ‘National Handicraft Development Programme 
(NHDP)’ that has 7 components namely (i) Ambedkar Hastshilp Vikas Yojana (Base Line 
Survey & Mobilization of artisans), (ii) Design & Technology Up gradation, (iii) Human 
Resource Development, (iv) Direct Benefit to Artisan, (v) Infrastructure and Technology 
Support, (vi) Research and Development and (vii) Marketing Support & Services.   In addition, 
Ministry of Textiles implements ‘Comprehensive Handicrafts Cluster Development Scheme 
(CHCDS)’ that has two components namely Mega Cluster & Special Projects under Integrated 
Development and Promotion of Handicraft (IDPH). 
 
        Ministry of Tourism under the Swadesh Darshan scheme provides financial assistance to 
the State Govt./UTs/Central Agencies for setting up projects as part of development of tourism 
infrastructure in the country.  Craft Haat/Craft Bazaar, Open Air Theatre/Amphi theatres, 
Souvenir Shops are set up under the scheme to help development of traditional arts in the 
country. 
  
Ministry of Minority Affairs is implementing a scheme titled USTTAD  (Upgrading the 
Skills and Training in Traditional Arts/ Crafts for Development) that aims at capacity building 
and upgrading the traditional skills of master craftsmen/artisans; training of minority youths in 
various identified traditional arts/crafts; develop national and international market linkages and 
preservation of languishing arts/crafts. Hunar Haat has been implemented as a component of this 
scheme which is an effective platform wherein opportunity is given to minority 
artisans/craftsmen and culinary experts from across the country to showcase and market their 
finest handicraft and exquisitely crafted indigenous products. 23 Hunar Haats have been 
organized since November, 2016 till December 2020 at different places. 
 
 Ministry of Rural Development under Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana-National Rural 
Livelihood Mission (DAY-NRLM) is implementing a scheme for promoting handloom and 
handicraft artisanal clusters. The scheme is being implemented in 13 States (Assam, Bihar, 
Chattisgarh, Gujarat, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, 
Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal). 
 
(b) & (c): No, sir.

(a) whether Government is aware of the fact that air pollution has become a serious threat

(b) if so, the details thereof;

(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor?

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARAS (a) TO (d) OF THE RAJYA 
SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 75 DUE FOR REPLY ON 08.02.2021 REGRADING 
COMBATING AIR POLLUTION RAISED BY SHRI KANAKAMEDALA RAVINDRA 
KUMAR, HON’BLE MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT 
(a) to (d)
Air pollution is presently one of the biggest environmental challenges globally. In 
India, Indo-gangetic plains have high air pollution levels due to adverse meteorology, 
dust due to alluvial soil, and sources such as vehicles, industries, construction & 
demolition activities, road dust, biomass burning, etc.  
The Government has taken several steps for mitigation of air pollution. Hon’ble Prime 
Minister launched Air Quality Index (AQI) in 2015, which provides air pollution 
information and health effect in simple form, which can be understood even by 
common persons. National Air Quality Standards are also based on health 
consideration.  
On 15 th August 2020, the Hon’ble Prime Minister also announced to improve air 
quality in more than 100 cities.  
Government of India launched National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), which is very 
comprehensive plan to tackle air pollution problem across the country in a focussed 
manner to achieve 20 % to 30 % reduction in PM 10 and PM 2.5levels by 2024 from 
2017 levels. The concerned ministries, State Governments, Research Institutes, 
Industries, etc. are partner in this effort. 
Based on air quality data, 122 non-attainment cities have been identified, and City 
Specific Clean Air Action Plans have been prepared and approved for 102 non-
attainment cities.The other measures taken by the Government includes: 
i. Vehicular Pollution Control
 Leapfrogging from BS-IV to BS-VI norms for fuel and vehicles since April,
2020.
 Network of Metro rails for public transport are enhanced and more cities are
covered.
 Development of Expressway and Highways are also reducing the fuel
consumption and pollution.
 Introduction of cleaner/alternate fuels like CNG, LPG, ethanol blending in
petrol.
 Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Electric Vehicles (FAME) -2 scheme
has been rolled out
 Permit requirement for electric vehicles has been exempted.
 Promotion of public transport and improvements in roads and building of
more bridges to ease congestion on roads.
ii. Industrial Pollution Control
 Stringent emission norms for Coal based Thermal Power Plants (TPPs).
 Pet coke and furnace oil have been banned as fuel in Delhi and NCR States.
137

 Industrial units shifting to PNG.
 Installation of on-line continuous monitoring devices in highly polluting
industries.
 Shifting of Brick kilns to zig-zag technology for reduction of pollution
iii. Waste Management
 Notifications of 6 waste management rules covering solid waste, plastic
waste, e-waste, bio-medical waste, C&D waste and hazardous waste.
 Setting up infrastructure such ass waste processing plants.
 Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) for plastic and e-waste management.
 Ban on burning of biomass/garbage.
iv. Crop Residue Management
 Under Central Sector Scheme on ‘Promotion of Agricultural Mechanization
for in-situ management of Crop Residue in the States of Punjab, Haryana,
Uttar Pradesh and NCT of Delhi’,agricultural machines and equipment for 
in-situ crop residue management are promoted with 50% subsidy to the 
individual farmers and 80% subsidy for establishment of Custom Hiring 
Centres.   
v. Monitoring of Air Quality
 Expansion of air quality monitoring network under National Air Quality
Monitoring Programme (NAMP)
 Implementation of Air Quality Early Warning System for Delhi. The system
provides alerts for taking timely actions.
vi. Allocation of funds
 ₹ 336.8 crores have been sanctioned to non-attainment cities under NCAP for
initiating actions such as expansion of monitoring network, construction and
demolition waste management facilities, non-motorised transport infrastructure,
green buffers, mechanical street sweepers, composting units etc.
 ₹2200 crores have been released in the Budget of FY 2020-21 to tackle the
burgeoning problem of air pollution. Further, an amount of 2,217 crores has

PRIVATISATION OF COAL SECTOR 
641. SHRI ELAMARAM KAREEM:
Will the Minister of COAL be pleased to state: 
(a) the reason behind the decision to allow private players in commercial mining of coal and
hundred percent Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in coal sector;
(b) whether Government would be able to regulate price of coal if the sector is privatized, if
so, mechanism thereof, if not, its impact on our economy;
(c) whether any studies have been conducted by the Government to assess impact of this
decision on sectors that use coal;
(d) its impact over electricity sector and whether increase in coal price would lead to increase
in electricity price; and
(e) whether Government has any plans to address such adverse impact?
ANSWER 
MINISTER OF PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS, COAL AND MINES 
(SHRI PRALHAD JOSHI) 
(a): 
Auction of coal mines for sale of coal would create a market place for coal with multiple 
producers to drive competition and adopt best practices in mining as well as environment 
management. The auction of coal mines for sale of coal in a transparent manner is expected 
to encourage transparent pricing of coal, based on the market forces. It would make 
maximum coal available in the market at the earliest. 
For sale of coal, allowing 100% FDI for coal mining activities including associated 
processing infrastructure is expected to attract international players 
and create efficient and 
competitive coal market. The nation will be enriched with the infusion of new technology and 
global best practices. 
(b): The coal price has been decontrolled w.e.f 01.01.2000. Consequently, coal companies are 
empowered to take decisions regarding pricing of coal. The Government does not play any 
role in it. 
 As per provisions under the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 [CMSP Act] 
and the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 [MMDR Act], there 
shall be no restriction to carry on mining operations for own consumption, sale or for any 
other purpose. The coal produced from the Coal Mine may be sold by the Successful Bidder 
in any manner as may be decided by the Successful Bidder including sale to affiliates and 
related parties, utilisation of coal for any purpose including but not limited to captive 
consumption, coal gasification, coal liquefaction and export of coal.  
WRITTEN ANSWERS TO UNSTARRED QUESTIONS
139

(c): A discussion paper on auction of coal mines for sale of coal containing key terms & 
conditions was published for Stakeholders’ consultation on 14.01.2020. Stakeholders’ 
consultations were held in Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai and Ranchi on 23.01.2020, 28.01.2020, 
29.01.2020 and 25.02.2020 respectively with coal consumer industries - Steel, Power, 
Cement etc. Stakeholders’ consultation with representatives of State Governments of 
Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, West Bengal, Jharkhand 
and Maharashtra was held on 05.02.2020 at New Delhi. 
 
  
(d) & (e): Commercial mining will bring more coal in the market which will reduce the 
demand-supply gap and encourage market determined prices. Auction of coal mines for sale 
of coal is expected to encourage transparent pricing of coal, based on the market forces. Any 
variation in coal cost directly varies the energy charges.

UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 656 
TO BE ANSWERED ON 08.02.2021 
  
Illegal coal mining in Meghalaya 
656.     SHRI RAKESH SINHA: 
Will the
 Minister of Coal be pleased to state :  
(a)      whether  it is a fact that illegal mining of coal in Meghalaya is continuing despite the ban 
by the National Green Tribunal (NGT);  
(b)      the steps being taken by Government to stop illegal mining there;  
(c )     the amount of loss it causes to Government; and  
(d)     whether it is also a fact that cement and power companies are hand in glove with illegal 
mining activities and they owe forty three crore rupees as fine which they have not deposited? 
ANSWER 
MINISTER OF PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS, COAL AND MINES 
(SHRI PRALHAD JOSHI) 
(a) & (b):         The State Government of Meghalaya has taken following measures to stop illegal 
coal mining  to ensure that no illegal mining of coal takes place in the State:- 
i) State Government has enforced provisions of the Mines and Minerals (Development & 
Regulation) Act, 1957 and cases are being registered under Section 21 of the Act against illegal 
coal mining. 
  
ii) The Authorised officers have been notified by Government under Section 21(4) of the MMDR 
Act, 1957 for
 seizing any mineral which has been mined or transported unlawfully along with 
vehicles, tools and equipments. 
  
iii) In exercise of power conferred under Section 22 of the MMDR Act, 1957, officers are 
authorised to make written complaint before Court for offences punishable under said act.  
 
 
iv) Strict instructions have been passed to Deputy Commissioners and Superintendent of Police 
to control illegal coal mining and enforce ban imposed by Hon’ble National Green Tribunal.  
 
 
v) The Government has been issuing prohibitory orders to stop illegal coal mining from time to 
time. 
167

vi) Patrolling and vigilance enhanced in coal bearing areas in order to prevent illegal extraction 
and transportation of coal. 
  
vii) Regular raids and surprise inspection of mines are being conducted by Joint Patrolling 
Teams and District Special Task Forces. 
viii) A Monitoring Committee under chairmanship of Chief Secretary constituted for monthly 
monitoring and review the actions taken and cases booked against illegal coal mining and 
transportation. 
ix) A Centralized Helpline Number has been created to receive complaints/information on illegal 
coal mining.  
x) Scheme has been introduced to provide Rs. 5000 Cash Reward to persons providing credible 
information on illegal coal mining. 
xi) Procedure has been laid down under the Section 21(5) of the MMDR Act, 1957 to recover 
illegally mined or illegally transported mineral and to recover price of mineral in case it is 
disposed. 
xii) Total 250 cases have been registered under Section 21 of the MMDR Act, 1957 since March, 
2019.
 
(c) & (d):  The amount of loss caused is Royalty @ Rs. 675 per MT and Cess @ Rs. 300 per 
MT.  There are no cases registered against cement and power companies for illegal coal mining. 
The Hon’ble National Green Tribunal vide order dated 17.01.2020 in OA No. 110(THC)/2012 
has directed the State to realise royalty, GST/VAT, contribution to the MEPR Fund and any 
other statutory tax and/levy payable on the illegally mined coal utilised by Cement 
Manufacturing Plants and the Thermal Power Plants in the State of Meghalaya after the ban on 
illegal rat-hole mining in the State of Meghalaya was imposed in April 2014 which comes to Rs. 
614 crores. Some Cement Plants have appealed to Hon’ble Supreme Court challenging the order 
and Hon’ble Supreme Court has orally observed that no action be taken by the State Government 
pursuant to demand notice issued for recovery of amount.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF COAL 
  
RAJYA SABHA 
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 658 
TO BE ANSWERED ON 08.02.2021 
 
Revision of coal royalty 
  
658 Dr. Sasmit Patra: 
  
     Will the Minister of Coal be pleased to state : 
  
a. the steps being undertaken by Government to revise coal royalty; and 
b. whether there are any plans to increase coal royalty for States like Odisha who 
contribute immensely? 
  
ANSWER 
  
MINISTER OF COAL, MINES AND PARLIAMENT AFFAIRS 
(SHRI PRALHAD JOSHI) 
  
( a)      Section 9(3) of the Mines and Mineral (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, 
provides that the Central Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, amend the 
second schedule (which specifies rates of royalty) so as to enhance or reduce the rate at which 
royalty shall be payable in respect of any mineral with effect from such date as may be 
specified in the notification, provided 
 that the Central Government shall not enhance the rate 
of royalty in respect of any mineral more than once during any period of three years. As such 
there is no mandatory provision in the act to revise the rates of royalty every three years. 
 
 
               However, a Study Group was constituted on 21.07.2014 for the purpose of 
examining the issue of revision of present royalty rates on coal and lignite. The Study Group 
had submitted its report suggesting no change in the rates of royalty. The suggestion of Study 
Group was accepted by the Government. 
 
 
Presently, the royalty is 14% per cent ad-valorem on price of coal being collected by 
the concerned State Government. In addition, contribution towards District Mineral 
Foundation (DMF) @ 30 % of the royalty in respect of mining leases, granted before 
12th January, 2015 and 10% of the royalty in respect of mining leases, granted on or after 
12th January, 2015, is also being collected by the concerned State Government. Further, due 
to ad-valorem nature of rates of royalty, there is increase in revenue to the coal producing 
States as and when the price of coal increases. 
 
 
(b)          Currently there are no plans to increase coal royalty for States like Odisha.

(a) whether it is a fact that most of the army men are under severe stress in the force losing more 
soldiers every year due to suicides, fratricides and untoward incidents on the borders; 
(b) if so, the reasons thereof and whether Government has any proposal to rehabilitate the 
soldiers for the last three years; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof?

studies by Defence Institute of Psychological  Research (DIPR).  Instances of fratricide are also 
not on the rise.

Nagar Van scheme 
 
672.  SHRI K.C. RAMAMURTHY: 
 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND CLIMATE CHANGE be pleased to 
state: 
 
(a)  the aims and objectives of Nagar Van scheme announced by the Ministry recently; 
(b)  the details of municipalities and corporations identified under the above scheme, with a    
particular reference to Karnataka; and 
(c)  the details of funds going to be arranged by the Ministry for this purpose and details of 
role of States, municipalities and corporations to develop forest in urban areas?  
 
 
ANSWER
 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND 
CLIMATE CHANGE 
(SHRI BABUL SUPRIYO) 
 
(a) The scheme 'Nagar Van Yojana (NVY) which was announced on 5 th June, 2020, 
aims at creation of 200 ‘city forests’ in urban cities having a Municipal Corporation 
or Municipalities, over a period of five years (2020-21 to 2024-25), primarily on 
forest land within the limits of municipalities.  Nagar Van may be developed over a 
minimum 10 ha to maximum 50 ha. area. The primary objective of NVY is to create 
a forested area within the city, to protect forest land from further degradation and 
encroachments thereby providing a healthy and wholesome living environment for 
the residents of the city. 
 
(b) A total of 18 Nagar Van Projects in 12 States including Karnataka State have been 
shortlisted for implementation initially under NVY, the details of which are given 
in Annexure.  
 
(c ) The total estimated cost of Nagar Van Yojna is Rs.415.00 crore for the period of 
2020-21 to 2024-25 for implementation from the National Funds under 
Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA). 
Scheme envisages providing Central funds of Rs. 2.0 crore per project for 
maximum of 50 ha area to meet the Cost of fencing, Soil-moisture conservation 
(SMC) measures, Administrative cost and Maintenance cost of plantation. The 
Nagar Vans are proposed to be developed in collaborative approach involving 
Forest department and other departments and agencies in the State/UT like NGOs, 
Corporate bodies, Industries, Civil Societies etc. The financial support from the 
Central Government is to meet cost of fencing, SMC measures etc., all other 
activities for developing the Nagar Van is to be done by collaboration of other 
agencies.

MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND CLIMATE CHANGE

UNSTARRED QUESTION No. 677 
TO BE ANSWERED ON 08.02.2021 
 
Deforestation of trees in Goa 
 
677 SHRI SANJAY SINGH: 
 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND CLIMATE CHANGE be pleased to 
state: 
 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government proposes to cut fifty thousand trees in two 
protected forest areas in Goa to make way for three central projects; 
(b) the details of the number of trees cut across the country during the last three years for 
various development purposes, year-wise, State/UT-wise; and 
(c) the action Government proposes to take to save the trees and forests at the altar of 
development? 
 
ANSWER
 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND 
CLIMATE CHANGE 
(SHRI BABUL SUPRIYO) 
 
(a)  All projects including central projects related to States/UTs including Goa which 
requires forest land are scrutinised and decision is takenby the Central Govt. as 
per procedure stipulated under the provisions ofForest (Conservation) Act (FCA), 
1980. Since April, 2020 twonumbers of projects (including central projects) have 
been accorded final approval under FCA, 1980 and 27,429 number of tress are 
stipulated to be removed.  
 
(b) In the last three years (i.e. 2017-18 to 2019-20)72 lakhs 4 thousand 97number of 
trees were stipulated to be removed and more than 17 crore 35 lakhs 3 thousand 
420 number of plants have been stipulated for plantation under compensatory 
afforestation. The year wise details of trees stipulated for removal are annexed. 
 
(c)  All the developmental projects for which forest area is required are scrutinised 
and decided as per the provisions of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. It is 
ascertained that minimum forest area which is inescapable, is diverted with all 
possible mitigative measures. To compensate the loss of trees and 
forest,necessary Compensatory Afforestation (CA) is ensured with the principle 
to compensate the loss of land by land and afforestation over the acquired land
.  
In addition, plantations are also taken up from the funds under Net Present Value 
(NPV) levied as additional compensation towards diversions. 
 
The trees are removed only when it is absolutely necessary. As per the 
Government policy, more trees are planted than number of trees approved for 
213

removal under Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. Because of this policy, India’s 
forest cover is increasing. As per the provisions of Forest (Conservation) Act, 
1980, Government of India accords prior permission for non-forest use of forest 
land. Such permissions are accorded subject to recommendation of the concerned 
State/UT Government and for unavoidable developmental projects/purposes. 
While according such permissions, it is ensured that minimum number of trees 
are removed which are inevitable.

Plastic Elimination and National Marine Litter Policy 
 
678. DR. NARENDRA JADHAV: 
 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND CLIMATE CHANGE be pleased to 
state: 
 
(a) whether as per Economic Advisory Council's report on Coastal Marine Spatial Planning 
and Tourism, Government has taken steps to draft a Plastic Elimination and National 
Marine Litter Policy, if so, the details thereof; 
(b) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) whether Government has taken any steps for enactment of suitable legislation and 
regulations for coastal regulation and planning along with policy guidelines for marine 
pollution and litter needs? 
 
 
ANSWER
 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND 
CLIMATE CHANGE 
(SHRI BABUL SUPRIYO) 
 
(a) to (c): The Ministry has already notified Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, and its 
amendments,through which plastic waste is managed in the country.The Ministry had also issued 
“Standard Guidelines for Single-Use Plastic” on 21st January 2019 to all States/UTs and 
Ministries. The Standard guidelines inter alia lay down waste management system 
improvements, legal options for States/Union Territories to prohibit Single Use Plastic items 
through regulatory measures etc. Apart from the regulations at the Central level, many State 
Governments through their own Notifications has imposed partial or full ban on use of plastic 
carry bags/single use plastic in their states. 
 
Separately, through the Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2011 several activities are 
prohibited in the CRZ areas like setting up and expansion of units or mechanism for disposal of 
wastes and effluents, except for some essential activities. Government of India has initiated 
several programmes such as “Swachh Bharat Abhiyan”, National Mission for Clean Ganga and 
Smart Cities Mission” in order to develop clean and sustainable environment. 
 
Society of Integrated Coastal Management (SICOM) under the Ministry of Environment, Forest 
and Climate Change has embarked upon a programme for the Beach Management Services 
(BEAMS) - Blue flag certification of beaches in each of the 13 coastal States /UTs including 
216

 
 
Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep islands under the Integrated Coastal Zone 
Management (ICZM) Programme, India. The main objective of setting up of BEAMS 
programme is to promote sustainable development in coastal regions of India for the beach 
management authorities to strive to achieve high international standards in four categories of: 
• Environmental Management including cleanliness  
• Solid waste management in beaches 
• Environment Education 
 
Eight beaches were awarded for the certification are: Kappad (Kerala), Shivrajpur (Gujarat), 
Ghoghla (Diu), Kasarkod and Padubidri (Karnataka), Rushikonda (Andhra Pradesh), Golden 
(Odisha) and Radhanagar (Andaman & Nicobar Islands). 
 
The Ministry has also constituted a Steering Committee on 14 th May 2019 in order to 
harmonize the efforts of various ministries/departments and agencies towards marine litter 
particularly due to plastic waste.

(a) whether Government has taken serious note of spread of invasive Lantana plants in tiger
habitats across India that has resulted in scarcity of native forage plants for wild
herbivores;
(b) whether Government has undertaken/plans to undertake any steps for ecological
restoration of Lantana invaded landscapes;
(c) if so, the details thereof including area restored till date out of total Lantana invaded area;
(d) if not, the reasons therefor;
(e) whether Government has commissioned any research to understand how native
vegetation responds to various Lantana removal practices like uprooting, weeding, fire,

(a), (b) & (c) Yes, the Government is aware of invasive species in tiger reserves of the country 
which are being mapped on a quadrennial basis during country wide assessment of tigers.  This 
mapping helps in formulating site specific interventions which are operationalised through the 
Tiger Conservation Plans mandated by the Wildlife (Protection) Act and financially assisted 
under the ongoing Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Project Tiger.

(e) & (f) Yes, the National Tiger Conservation Authority in collaboration with the Wildlife
Institute of India has initiated a project titled “Study on vegetation and habitat quality changes
